metaDescription: Own mineral rights near Wright, WY in the Powder River Basin? We buy coal-adjacent and CBM/oil mineral interests. Deed history checked before any offer.
heroLead: Wright was built by ARCO as a company town to run the coal mines around it, and mineral ownership out here is almost never simple - coal, coalbed methane, and conventional oil and gas can sit under the same section held by three different owners.
intro: Wright came up in the 1970s as a planned town to support the Black Thunder and Jacobs Ranch mine operations, and Campbell County around it has been the single largest coal-producing county in the country for decades. But coal isn't the only thing under this ground - the same acreage has coalbed methane history from the CBM boom of the late 1990s and 2000s, and conventional Powder River Basin oil zones sit deeper still.

That layering is exactly why mineral ownership here is rarely one clean deed. It's common to find the coal severed to one party, oil and gas rights held separately by another, and a small legacy CBM royalty interest from the boom years sitting on top of both, all tied to the same quarter section.

sections.heading: Coal, CBM, and Split Estate Around Wright
paragraphs: A lot of Campbell County coal is federally owned and leased through BLM competitive coal leasing, which means the surface rancher, the coal mineral owner, and the oil and gas mineral owner can be three entirely different parties on the same tract. If your family homesteaded ranch ground here, there's a real chance you kept the oil and gas rights even if the coal underneath was already federal, or reserved separately generations ago.

The CBM boom left its own mark. Wells drilled in the late 1990s through the mid-2000s across the Powder River Basin dewatered coal seams to release methane, and a lot of those wells have gone through steep decline or been plugged entirely as the boom went bust. If you're holding a royalty interest from that era, the check you're getting now, if you're getting one at all, is likely a fraction of what it was fifteen years ago.

sections.heading: What Owning Minerals Near Wright Usually Means
paragraphs: Most private mineral interests we see around Wright trace back to ranch homesteads that predate the town itself, with rights split off through a coal lease, an oil and gas lease, or both at different points. Some owners hold only the oil and gas, with coal already tied up under federal lease. Others hold a small legacy CBM royalty that barely moves the needle anymore but still generates a check and a tax form every year.

sections.heading: How We Approach an Offer Here
paragraphs: We start by sorting out exactly what estate you hold - oil and gas, coal, or both - since Campbell County split estate isn't unusual and it changes the whole valuation. If there's CBM or conventional oil royalty history, we look at the actual decline curve rather than the last check amount, because post-boom CBM interests especially can look deceiving if you only glance at recent numbers. Any offer we give reflects that real production trend, not a flat guess.

faqs.question: Do I own coal, oil and gas, or both under my land near Wright?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on your deed history. Split estate is common in Campbell County, and we sort out exactly what you hold before making any offer.

faqs.question: My coalbed methane royalty checks have dropped a lot over the years. Is the interest still worth anything?
faqs.answer: Often yes, though typically less than during the CBM boom years. We look at your current decline curve rather than assuming based on peak-era numbers.

faqs.question: Is federal BLM coal leasing the same as my private oil and gas rights?
faqs.answer: No, they're usually separate. Federal coal leasing in Campbell County doesn't affect privately held oil and gas minerals under the same tract unless your specific deed says otherwise.

faqs.question: How do you value an interest with mixed coal, CBM, and conventional history?
faqs.answer: We evaluate each mineral estate you actually hold separately, weighing production history and current activity for that specific right rather than lumping everything into one number.
